articles.title: Institutional memory: keeping the 'why' alive when people and agents change the system
articles.summary: A configuration tells you what an AI workflow does today, not why it was built that way. The Rationale Ledger keeps the reasons, especially the boundaries, alive through staff turnover and edits.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Mission first, then one real task: how small nonprofit teams make AI stick
articles.summary: Small, mission-driven teams adopt AI when it is tied to the mission, started with one tool and three named tasks for thirty days, kept as a repeated habit, and scaled only once on-mission is agreed.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Recurring reports and updates for many audiences: write once, adapt with AI
articles.summary: Weekly reports, audience summaries, translations and board or donor updates become far quicker when you keep one source of truth, specify the audience's question, and check accuracy once upstream.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Repeatable AI workflows for small teams: grants, donor updates, meetings, field reports
articles.summary: Brief the tool on mission, audience and constraints, feed it real inputs, and have a person who knows the facts check every claim before a grant, donor update, meeting recap or field report goes out.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Making AI adoption stick: real work, short sessions, two conversations
articles.summary: Adoption stalls when a rollout ends at licences and a webinar, so design for real tasks with deadlines, a thirty-minute first session, separate handling for enthusiasts and sceptics, and a recurring check.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: The apprenticeship problem: what happens to junior roles when AI writes the first draft
articles.summary: The first draft was never the product of junior work; it was how juniors became seniors. The Draft, Review, Own ladder keeps that learning route open while AI takes the routine tasks.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: What AI fluency actually means: the 4Ds after a hundred days of practice
articles.summary: AI fluency is not tool knowledge, speed or confidence. It is one habit, ask for something specific and check it against what you know, and the 4Ds show where that habit takes real work.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: The middle-manager squeeze: where AI adoption actually stalls
articles.summary: Executives set the ambition and staff do the work, but managers decide whether the two connect. The Four Pressures map shows where AI adoption stalls and what leaders can do about each pressure.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Reinvention or change management? When the playbook is the wrong tool
articles.summary: Change management assumes the work is right; AI sometimes changes what the work should be. The Reinvention Threshold uses two questions and four responses to sort each task in a fortnight.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The near-miss log: AI risk management small organisations will actually keep
articles.summary: A risk register lists what might go wrong; a near-miss log records what nearly did. Notice, name, narrow: a one-page habit that teaches a small organisation more about its real AI exposure.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The audit trail for an AI-influenced decision: what to record and for how long
articles.summary: When AI helped shape a decision and a funder asks how it was reached, "we have the chat history" is not an answer. The Decision Ledger: four lines, five minutes, one named owner.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Before you trust an experimental AI feature in production: the client's checklist
articles.summary: A new AI feature arrives labelled experimental. Do you adopt or refuse? Neither. The Trust Ladder moves a feature from sandbox to standard in five steps, with a fallback and a named owner at each.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Advice or sales pitch? Five tests for any AI recommendation, including ours
articles.summary: Everyone advising on AI has something to sell, including us. The Five-Test Screen checks incentive, evidence, alternatives, scope-out and reversibility, so a board can tell advice from a pitch.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Leading an AI-enabled team: teach checking first, judge decisions, measure more
articles.summary: Managers get better AI work by teaching verification before features, learning the core terms, making judgment visible, reviewing decisions as well as output, and measuring time recovered.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Vendor concentration and the exit plan: diversify AI suppliers without doubling cost
articles.summary: One AI supplier means one set of prices, terms and roadmaps. The Portability Ladder tests four things: method, data, workflow and account control. Diversify by being able to move, not by buying twice.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Calibrating trust in AI: diagnose the limit, match scrutiny to the stakes
articles.summary: Treat trust as something that moves with the task: name the specific limit behind a failure, watch for drift outside a tool's reliable zone, and scale your checking to the cost of being wrong.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Pilot theatre: why AI demos succeed and production fails
articles.summary: Why do AI pilots impress and production disappoint? Because most pilots are built to show it can work, not whether it will. The Three-Gap Test: material, people and ownership.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Blast radius: designing what an automation can reach
articles.summary: Before connecting an agent to a new system, ask what it could reach on its worst day. Grant access per task rather than per agent, and separate read, write and send, so one mistake stays contained.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Browser agents in a logged-in session: should you allow them at all?
articles.summary: A browser agent in a logged-in session inherits everything that login can reach. Judge the session, not the task, and default to no where irreversible or highly sensitive actions are available.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Checking AI output before it ships: five habits that cost minutes, not afternoons
articles.summary: Read AI drafts as an editor, own what carries your name, check against the goal as well as the instruction, and build thirty-second checks and checkpoints into the work.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Cost per completed task: the unit economics of AI nobody reports
articles.summary: Most AI business cases quote a licence fee and hours saved. Neither is a unit cost. Our view: measure the cost of one accepted output, including failed attempts, review and rework. The Completed-Task Ledger explains how.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Human-in-the-loop, and where the human actually adds value
articles.summary: Human review only protects you if it sits where an agent's confidence and competence diverge, before output is polished into fluent prose. Batch approvals and late reviews are oversight in name only.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Indirect injection: your own document store is an attack surface
articles.summary: To an agent that reads it, any shared drive or ticket system many people could edit is untrusted content. Scope read access, curate trusted sources and log what the agent reads.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Named owner, operating guide, test set: what makes an agent survive its author
articles.summary: An agent only its builder understands is a personal project running in production. A named owner, a written operating guide and a periodic test set are the minimum bar before calling it finished.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Prompt injection explained for executives and DPOs who will never write a filter
articles.summary: Prompt injection hides instructions in content an agent reads, and OWASP ranks it the top LLM risk. A plain-language explanation, a vendor's own test figures, and layered defences any organisation can apply.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Time saved is not value: turning hours into capacity, outcomes and budget lines
articles.summary: Everyone says AI saves them two hours a week. Nobody can spend that answer. The Value Conversion Ladder turns hours into capacity, outcomes and budget lines a board can act on.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Agent, skill or tool: what to build and what each really costs
articles.summary: A tool, a skill and an agent cost very different amounts to build, run and govern. One question, whether the task must decide what happens next, tells you which one to choose.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI theatre: why leadership announcements change nothing, and what does
articles.summary: A launch event is not adoption. We call the gap AI theatre. Announce, Enable, Embed is a quick diagnostic for which layer your effort is missing, and what leaders can do.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Why one paid AI assistant used daily beats hopping between free tiers
articles.summary: The productivity gain from paying for an assistant comes from removing limits that make you ration it, so commit to one tool, then carry your prompts and trust habits across if you ever switch.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: The tasks we will never automate with an agent, and why the list is short but absolute
articles.summary: A short, absolute list of tasks no agent should be configured to do: safeguarding referrals, eligibility decisions, payment authorisation and public statements on live matters, where the human is the safeguard.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Write the method before you buy the agent
articles.summary: If nobody can write down in plain steps how a task is done today, buying an agent for it is premature. The written method is the real readiness test, and it surfaces hidden disagreements early.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Choosing an AI tool: start with where the work lives, not a ranking
articles.summary: Three questions about the task in front of you pick between Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini faster than any feature chart, and a team should settle its workflow before debating which tool to standardise on.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Five questions every board should ask about AI this quarter
articles.summary: Trustees do not need a technical briefing. They need five questions asked every quarter, with evidence. Here is the Quarterly Five, with the answers that should worry you.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: ISO/IEC 42001 for organisations that will never certify
articles.summary: Why most small NGOs and foundations should not pursue ISO/IEC 42001 certification, and which parts of the AI management system standard are worth borrowing as a structural checklist.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: NIST AI RMF applied to a 60-person NGO
articles.summary: How a 60-person NGO can apply NIST's four AI RMF functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) at proportionate size, with a paragraph per tool and a review question instead of dashboards.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: OECD and UNESCO principles: what they actually oblige you to do
articles.summary: The OECD and UNESCO AI principles are not legally binding on an NGO, but they shape regulation and partner expectations; treat them as a values-alignment check and cite them only with specific practices.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Copilot in Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel and PowerPoint, and when to reach for Claude
articles.summary: Each Microsoft 365 app has one habit worth learning and one place it needs a human check, and a simple rule tells you when to use Copilot, when to use Claude, and when neither settles the question.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Copilot is a habit problem: the specific-ask routine to teach your team first
articles.summary: Teams get value from Microsoft 365 Copilot when they learn to name the audience, goal and format, treat the first output as a draft, know its failure modes, and keep a hard line on sensitive data.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Documentation is not certification, and saying so is an advantage
articles.summary: Why an internally maintained AI governance file should be called documentation, not certification: the precise label survives follow-up questions from boards, funders and auditors, and matches what the law asks.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Re-scoring AI readiness: theatre if nobody acted on the first score?
articles.summary: A second AI readiness score only counts as evidence if specific interventions followed specific findings from the first; otherwise it measures whether someone remembered to run the survey again.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: What an auditor, a board and a funder each actually ask for
articles.summary: Auditors, boards and funders ask to see your AI governance file for different reasons; keep one evidence file but prepare a short cover framing for each audience.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: When AI shapes the decision, who signs it? Accountability that survives an audit
articles.summary: When AI ranks, drafts or acts, whose signature is on it? The Influence Ladder sorts AI involvement into four rungs and three questions every signer should answer.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: DPIA and AI: when an impact assessment is triggered
articles.summary: A practical trigger test for when an AI use case needs a data protection impact assessment, so a DPO does a few properly instead of running one on everything or none at all.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The five artefacts of an AI governance evidence file
articles.summary: The five documents that together let an organisation prove its AI governance to an auditor, board or funder: policy, tool inventory, training record, competency assessment and review record.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: What "personal data" means once a prompt leaves the building
articles.summary: Personal data is wider than names and numbers, and a prompt's fate depends on account tier, retention and sub-processors; a technical explainer for DPOs and IT leads, with four questions to ask any tool.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Beneficiary data and AI: the question with no comfortable answer
articles.summary: Both sides of the argument on putting beneficiary data into AI tools, and a conservative default: keep it out unless genuinely de-identified, with named sign-off every time.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Disclosing AI use to funders: when you must, should, and when it backfires
articles.summary: When disclosing AI use to funders is required, when it is good practice, and when vague or excessive disclosure backfires, with the rule to name the task and the safeguard.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI safeguarding language checks: build the rulebook once, apply it every time
articles.summary: How to build a dedicated AI check that compares external content against a written safeguarding communications rulebook, with a named human for borderline and consent questions.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Annexes: why casework, fundraising, HR and procurement need their own rules
articles.summary: Keep one shared AI policy core and add short annexes only for casework, fundraising, HR and procurement, where risk genuinely diverges, changing content but never the shared structure.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI policy escalation path and the 24-hour rule
articles.summary: What to write into an AI policy for the moment something goes wrong: one named contact, a broad definition of escalation-worthy, no penalty for reporting, and a fixed 24-hour clock from discovery.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI policy review: the six-month cycle and what triggers an early one
articles.summary: Why an AI policy needs a fixed six-month review against four specific questions, plus four yes-or-no triggers (departed contact, changed tool, repeated escalation, changed law) that force an earlier one.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Who owns AI here? The operating model a 300-person organisation actually needs
articles.summary: Most organisations cannot say who owns AI. A 300-person organisation needs five named seats (Sponsor, Steward, Use Owners, Champions, Assurer), filled starting with the Steward, to replace the default of nobody.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI permitted use by role: the four-column table that does the work
articles.summary: A template for the permitted-use table in an AI policy: one row per role and task, with four columns for role, task, safeguard and data boundary, so staff can find answers in seconds.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI policy red lines: the decisions that never get delegated
articles.summary: A short checklist of decisions an AI policy should never delegate, such as ending employment, safeguarding judgements and legal signatures, and why keeping the list short protects the rest of the policy.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Write your AI policy permissions first, not the prohibitions
articles.summary: Why an AI policy should open with specific permissions, each naming the task, the safeguard and the data boundary in one sentence, instead of leading with a list of prohibitions staff will route around.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Why most AI work tasks go slowly, and a four-step method that fixes it
articles.summary: AI-assisted tasks run fast when you name the output format first, make the model flag ambiguity, treat the first result as a draft you check against the source, and pick one small workflow to repeat.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Before and after the meeting: AI workflows for prep, follow-up and action plans
articles.summary: Meeting prep in minutes, same-day follow-up emails, hour-long training sessions and workshop notes turned into owned actions all work with AI when you ask for the right few outputs and add the personal detail yourself.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: AI for board papers: encode the structure, write the judgement fresh
articles.summary: Encode the four-part board paper structure (decision, options, risk, recommendation) as a standing agent workflow, but have the accountable person write the decision, rejected option, risk owner and sign-off each time.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Plain-language rewriting: the highest-value low-risk task in the sector
articles.summary: Why plain-language rewriting is one of the safest, highest-value uses of AI in the sector, what a good rewrite keeps, and the side-by-side check that catches quiet meaning loss.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI translation: delegate the first draft, keep the review with a bilingual human
articles.summary: Fluent AI mistranslations are invisible to anyone who cannot read both languages, so delegate only the first draft and have a named bilingual reviewer check it sentence by sentence.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Decision-ready documents from raw material: briefs, memos, decks and dashboards
articles.summary: Briefs, memos, benchmarks, decks, dashboards and data stories get faster when you settle the decision and the key takeaways first, then let AI do the sorting and layout, and verify every claim.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: AI-assisted research a programme officer can defend
articles.summary: How a programme officer can use AI to surface sources faster while keeping every claim traceable: quote the passage, open each source, and treat suggested citations as leads until verified.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Donor and funder intelligence without a compliance incident
articles.summary: Which donor and funder research with AI is safe public-source work, and where compiling wealth estimates or personal characteristics on a named individual becomes personal data processing needing sign-off.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Monitoring and evaluation: where AI helps and where it corrupts the data
articles.summary: AI can draft M&E narrative and charts from settled data, but outlier calls, gap-filling, causal claims and summary categories must stay human or the dataset is quietly corrupted.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Before and after: one grant report with AI, honestly measured
articles.summary: A worked example of redesigning a six-hour foundation grant report with AI, where checking time nets the saving down to two honest hours rather than a vendor's headline claim.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Context engineering vs prompt engineering
articles.summary: Once a task is repeated or built into an agent, what content reaches the model matters more than how the prompt is worded, and retrieved content must be treated as untrusted.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The four checks before anything leaves the building
articles.summary: Four targeted checks to run before AI-assisted work leaves the building, covering sources, boundary cases, judgement calls and omissions, without redoing the whole task by hand.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Prompt patterns that survive contact with real documents
articles.summary: Four structural prompt patterns that hold up on messy real documents, including showing the actual template, naming what to ignore, requesting uncertainty flags and chunking long files.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Task decomposition for AI: finding the handover point
articles.summary: How to break a task into steps and write down the handover point, usually just before the first judgement call, where AI output ends and human responsibility begins.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The verification tax: what checking costs, and when it exceeds the gain
articles.summary: Checking AI output has a real time cost that productivity claims omit, and this piece shows how to price it and when it cancels out the saving.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Fundraising AI playbook revisited: what changed after twelve months
articles.summary: A year after publishing our fundraising playbook, what real use corrected, including a second axis for how personal a message claims to be, bundled prospect research, mid-level donor trust and ownership.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI playbook for Legal, Protection, IT and Procurement: what to delegate, what to keep
articles.summary: How to split Legal, Protection, IT and Procurement work between routine tasks AI can draft or triage and decisions that must stay human, such as safeguarding disclosures, contract sign-off and access grants.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The unit of AI value is a task, never a job
articles.summary: Why AI adoption decisions should be made task by task rather than for a whole job or department, and how a task inventory replaces the blanket yes or no.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI playbook for Communications and Advocacy: what to delegate, what to keep
articles.summary: Which Communications and Advocacy tasks to delegate to AI, such as first-draft posts, media digests and scheduling, and which never to hand over, including crisis response, policy positions and sensitive press contact.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI playbook for HR: the department where most red lines live
articles.summary: Which HR tasks can be delegated to AI, such as scheduling, job posting drafts and aggregated survey themes, and why hiring, discipline, grievances and individual personal data stay with named humans.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI playbook for Leadership and Governance: what to delegate, what to keep
articles.summary: Which Leadership and Governance tasks can be delegated to AI, such as board report compilation and decision briefs, and why strategic decisions, risk sign-off and executive personnel choices cannot be.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI playbook for Finance and Administration: what to delegate, what to keep
articles.summary: Which Finance and Administration tasks to delegate to AI, such as first-pass reconciliation and drafting, and which never to hand over, including authorising payments, signing year-end statements and investigating irregularities.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI playbook for Programmes and Monitoring: five to delegate, three never
articles.summary: Five Programmes and Monitoring tasks worth delegating to AI, including survey summaries and indicator cross-referencing, and three that never should be, including interpreting beneficiary feedback and signing off outcomes.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: When leadership is the least fluent group in the building
articles.summary: Leaders often have the least hands-on AI experience, which caps adoption, and training them well takes a private setting, strategic framing, a peer facilitator and explicit permission to ask basic questions.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The attendance record: trivial to keep, impossible to reconstruct
articles.summary: A training attendance record takes thirty seconds to keep and cannot be rebuilt later, so capture who attended, when, what was covered and at what level, including contractors.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Training breadth vs behavioural depth: the trade-off nobody prices
articles.summary: Spreading training thinly across everyone gives a good completion rate but rarely moves anyone past guided use, while depth costs visibility; here is how to decide where the hours go.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Why the playbook belongs to the team, not the trainer
articles.summary: A playbook written by the trainer goes stale quickly, so have the team write and own its own, updated the week an exception appears, even if the first version is rough.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Reading a vendor benchmark without being taken in
articles.summary: Why a vendor's headline benchmark is a hypothesis rather than evidence, and the four questions to ask about who chose the task and the success measure before it influences a purchase.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The seven capability levels, and why Level 3 is the floor
articles.summary: A seven-level ladder of AI capability from awareness to practice-shaping, and the case for judging training by how many staff reach Level 3, independent competent use.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: When the honest answer is "you do not need AI for this"
articles.summary: Some tasks do not need AI, such as rare, already-fast, one-off or unrecoverable ones, and saying no for stated reasons makes later recommendations more believable.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Before/after measurement without surveillance
articles.summary: How to get the baseline a pilot needs by measuring tasks in aggregate rather than timing named individuals, so staff do not start performing for the metric.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The pilot that produces evidence instead of anecdote
articles.summary: A pilot produces evidence rather than anecdote only if four things are fixed in writing beforehand, namely a success metric, a measured baseline, an end date and a named honest reporter.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Which department should pilot AI first? Four questions to ask
articles.summary: Choose the first AI pilot department for task volume, recoverable risk and a manager who already measures things, not for enthusiasm or external pressure.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI readiness dimensions 4-6: verification, logging, data protection
articles.summary: What a low score looks like on verification, logging and data protection, with a quick diagnostic for each and why data protection needs continuing oversight rather than a one-off fix.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI readiness dimensions 7-10: workforce impact, politics, safety, future-readiness
articles.summary: What low scores on workforce impact, internal politics, psychological safety and future-readiness look like, why they stall adoption, and why they move only when leadership changes its behaviour.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Ground rules for team AI use: what not to paste, what to say, what to call things
articles.summary: Three things a manager can set in an afternoon: a specific list of what never goes into a chat, a norm of disclosing AI use, and five agreed terms so meetings stop talking past each other.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Prompt in short, checked steps: one ask, a plain start, specific feedback
articles.summary: Four habits that beat prompt formulas: one outcome per prompt, a plain first attempt, feedback specific enough to act on, and a real check on every number, date and quote the AI gives you.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: Scoring 62 out of 100: what a mid-range score means and what to do first
articles.summary: A mid-range readiness score of 62 can describe very different organisations, so read the ten-dimension breakdown, pick one dimension to move this quarter, and choose it using four criteria.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: AI readiness dimensions 1-3: fluency, delegation practice, description discipline
articles.summary: What a low score looks like on fluency, delegation practice and description discipline, with one quick diagnostic each and a realistic view of how long each takes to fix.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Stop re-explaining yourself: when to use a Project and when to build a Skill
articles.summary: A Project holds standing context, a Skill holds a repeatable process; this guide shows how to set up each, what to put in, and how to turn five manual steps into a Skill.
articles.author: Mamdouh Alqudsi

articles.title: The ten AI readiness dimensions, named and explained
articles.summary: The ten dimensions behind an AI readiness score, named and explained in plain language, from fluency and verification to psychological safety, and how they cluster into practice and climate.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: What a readiness score is actually measuring
articles.summary: An AI readiness score is a point-in-time snapshot, not a grade, forecast or benchmark, and its single number hides which of the ten dimensions is dragging it down.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Data classification from zero: what can go into an AI tool
articles.summary: A one-page, four-class scheme (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) and a single who-is-harmed test that tell staff what can go into a general-purpose AI tool.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The AI tool inventory: the least glamorous artefact that unlocks everything else
articles.summary: A five-column spreadsheet of the AI tools staff actually use is the prerequisite for any policy or assessment, and it only works if built in an amnesty spirit.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: What a language model cannot do, stated plainly
articles.summary: A plain list of what a language model cannot do, from not knowing your organisation to not being accountable, so staff can judge each task rather than rely on belief.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The 19-point problem: AI made consultants worse at one task in the study everyone quotes
articles.summary: In the Harvard study of 758 consultants, AI users were 25% faster but 19 percentage points less likely to reach the correct answer on a task outside the tool's competence, which reframes training.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: Article 4 of the EU AI Act was amended. The wording you were told to comply with is gone
articles.summary: Article 4 of the EU AI Act no longer requires organisations to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy; it now requires measures to support it, so documents quoting the old wording need revising.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: "Deployer" is the word that puts you in scope
articles.summary: Organisations that do not build AI systems are still deployers under the EU AI Act if staff use AI tools in their work, which puts them within scope of Article 4.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting

articles.title: The Omnibus delayed high-risk rules and rewrote Article 4. Neither is a reason to wait
articles.summary: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved the high-risk dates to December 2027 and August 2028 and rewrote Article 4 as a duty to support AI literacy, so AI literacy work is still due but the legal exposure is lighter.
articles.author: M.A.I. Consulting
